publicationDetails.journalName: Center for Latin American & Latino Studies (CLALS) Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This article offers a meta-analysis of a survey designed and implemented to explore the sociodemographic characteristics of potential migrants from the Eastern part of El Salvador. Because the survey was also intended to investigate the role of climate change as a possible driver of migration, it presents an opportunity to identify some methodological challenges in nascent research on the climate-migration nexus in Central America’s Northern Triangle. Examining our survey design and results, we draw attention to the following issues for researchers hoping to better understand climatic factors as drivers of migration: 1. how climatic factors can fall out of survey results, 2. the value of using available data sources in advance to determine climate affected populations as research subjects, 3. challenges of step migration and avoiding recency bias, 4. accounting for slow-onset climate impacts, 5. benefits of eliciting complete personal migration histories, 6. the value of rapid
ethnography to incorporate local discourses about the environment as a part of survey design.

title: Constitutional Stewardship: Executive Power, Legitimacy, and Institutional Durability in an Era of Permanent Crisis

detail.title: Constitutional Stewardship: Executive Power, Legitimacy, and Institutional Durability in an Era of Permanent Crisis
detail.abstract: Contemporary democratic executives govern in conditions of persistent crisis, declining public trust, accelerated information warfare, and heightened judicial scrutiny. Existing theories of executive power-ranging from strong executive models to procedural minimalism-struggle to reconcile decisiveness with legitimacy, adaptability with restraint, and crisis action with constitutional durability. This article introduces Constitutional Stewardship as a governing philosophy that reconceptualizes executive power as custodial responsibility for constitutional legitimacy, institutional continuity, and democratic consent-especially under conditions of crisis and uncertainty. Drawing on constitutional law, democratic legitimacy theory, public administration ethics, crisis governance research, and decision science, the article articulates a set of design principles that operationalize restraint, learning, and legitimacy as enforceable features of executive governance. Constitutional Stewardship offers a framework for evaluating executive action beyond outcomes alone and provides a system-level response to recurring patterns of executive failure in modern democracies.

title: Prosperity, Status Signal Inflation, and the Moralized Decline of Complex Societies

detail.title: Prosperity, Status Signal Inflation, and the Moralized Decline of Complex Societies
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a micro-founded theoretical model to explain the internal and gradual decline of complex societies at high levels of prosperity and security. Existing accounts often rely on macro-structural variables or teleological narratives and lack a clear linkage between individual motivations and systemic outcomes. The model integrates insights from status competition, sexual selection, and political sociology. It argues that when key status signals-material wealth for men and reproductive success for women-lose their differential value under conditions of widespread prosperity, individuals adapt their behavior in ways that unintentionally transform moral norms, political incentives, and institutional capacities. The resulting dynamics include the migration of status competition toward moral signaling, the rise of care-centered ethics and moral universalism, redistributive populism, fiscal stress, identity delegitimation, and declining internal and external security. These processes are not treated as ideological projects but as emergent outcomes of aggregated individual responses to changing incentives. The model is stress-tested through comparative references to the late Roman Empire, imperial China, and other historical cases, as well as through partial counterexamples. The paper does not offer deterministic predictions but identifies conditional mechanisms that generate recurrent vulnerabilities in prosperous civilizations.

title: Adaptive Recursive Dimensional Compression (ARDC): A Scaling Law for Emergent Efficiency

detail.title: Adaptive Recursive Dimensional Compression (ARDC): A Scaling Law for Emergent Efficiency

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human subjects, patient data, or participant interaction. All analyses are conducted on synthetic data, publicly available benchmark datasets, or simulated systems. As such, no ethics approval or informed consent was required.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Recursive Dimensional Compression (ARDC): a measurable efficiency relation for controlled recursion in learning and decision systems. ARDC models the tradeoff between redundancy removal and information decay by defining efficiency E(n) = 2−(n−1)MnC2 n Kn µn , (1) where n is recursion depth, Mn is informational mass (effective dimension), Cn is clarity (bounded coherence proxy), Kn is knowledge integrity (retained task relevant performance), and µn is uncertainty load (strictly positive risk/entropy proxy). The key claim is operational: recursion should be audited and stopped when marginal efficiency gains are exhausted under integrity constraints, rather than pushed deeper by default. Empirical results and controller demonstrations show a consistent crossover behavior: when redundancy removal dominates information decay, recursion transitions from destructive compression to adaptive abstraction, yielding higher performance-per-cost. ARDC therefore acts as a falsifiable stopping law that links information structure, computational cost, and governed recursion depth.

title: Nexus Between Economic Development, Energy Poverty and ICT in Bangladesh

detail.title: Nexus Between Economic Development, Energy Poverty and ICT in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: This paper examines the correlation between energy poverty, population, and internet use and the economic development of Bangladesh based on data in the World Bank between 2000 and 2019. Unit root test and Granger Causality test were used to determine whether these factors affect each other. Despite the fact that the GDP of Bangladesh has been increasing substantially, the access to electricity has been sporadic. It has become universal and hence is reliable and affordable, but this has been a challenge. The internet is being used by more people but the mobile towers require a constant supply of electricity and this has become a challenge to businesses and even to the homes. The outcome reveals that GDP has an impact on the access to electricity and the number of internet users has an impact on the access to electricity.

title: The Legitimacy Divergence Diagnostic (LDD): A Preventive Framework for Detecting Institutional Drift in Legal Systems

detail.title: The Legitimacy Divergence Diagnostic (LDD): A Preventive Framework for Detecting Institutional Drift in Legal Systems
detail.abstract:
Across common law jurisdictions, legal reform demonstrates a recurring tendency toward reactivity, emerging after tragedy, public scandal, or visible system failure rather than through preventive institutional assessment. This paper introduces the Legitimacy Divergence Diagnostic (LDD), a non-justiciable, limitation-aware framework designed to identify early divergence between procedural legal order and lived justice outcomes before institutional legitimacy erosion becomes externally visible.

The LDD operates as a meta-legal diagnostic tool rather than a doctrine of law, regulatory instrument, or adjudicative standard. It does not assess individual guilt, adjudicative correctness, or institutional intent, nor does it attribute fault to specific actors. Instead, it examines how cumulative asymmetries—between authority and accountability, order and mercy, and abstraction and lived experience—can gradually hollow institutional legitimacy despite sustained formal compliance with legal standards.

Drawing on law-and-society research, institutional burnout literature, and comparative justice reform analysis, the paper argues that legitimacy erosion is often detectable well in advance of crisis, yet remains structurally unaddressed due to the absence of early-warning diagnostics within legal governance frameworks.

To ground the framework empirically, the paper foregrounds a proposed New South Wales youth justice pilot program, focusing on remand overuse and the overrepresentation of Aboriginal youth. The pilot outlines a controlled, evaluative application of the LDD as a preventive legitimacy assessment tool, integrating diversionary pathways, institutional self-audit indicators, and measurable outcome metrics, including recidivism, remand duration, practitioner wellbeing, and community trust. The pilot is explicitly falsifiable: if no measurable improvement is observed relative to matched control cohorts, the LDD hypothesis is subject to revision or rejection.

The paper concludes that the LDD offers legal institutions a disciplined method for preventive self-correction that preserves institutional legitimacy while reducing long-term harm. By enabling reform prior to crisis, the framework seeks to strengthen—not undermine—the ethical resilience, public confidence, and adaptive capacity of the rule of law.

reference: Harvard Business School Accounting & Management Unit Working Paper No. 25-057
title: Customer-Facing Technologies and Banks' Macroeconomic Information Production
affiliations: HKUST Business School, Harvard Business School, Columbia University - Columbia Business School and

detail.title: Customer-Facing Technologies and Banks' Macroeconomic Information Production

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School Accounting & Management Unit Working Paper No. 25-057

detail.abstract: We examine whether technologies deployed in banks’ customer-facing functions improve their ability to produce information about future macroeconomic conditions. Although primarily adopted to enhance customer engagement, these technologies, such as web analytics and behavioral tracking software, allow banks to collect timely and granular data from a broad base of customers that inform assessments of local economic conditions. Using a novel measure of customer-facing technology adoption derived from banks’ website source code, we find that banks with greater adoption produce loan loss provisions that are more informative about future regional economic activity. This effect is driven by technologies that collect macro-relevant data and is stronger for banks with larger and more digitally engaged customer bases, for banks operating in more economically volatile regions, and for banks with greater data-related human capital. We further find that banks with greater adoption of customer-facing technologies experience smaller increases in nonperforming loans following adverse macroeconomic changes and disclose more macroeconomic content in regulatory filings and conference calls. Overall, our findings highlight a distinct informational role of customer-facing technologies in banks’ forecasting, risk management, and financial reporting.

title: Addressing the “Chicken-and-Egg” Dilemma: Pension Reform, Market Coordination, and Policy Design
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Addressing the “Chicken-and-Egg” Dilemma: Pension Reform, Market Coordination, and Policy Design
detail.abstract: Why do domestic stock markets in many emerging market economies fail to develop, even in the presence of high savings rates? We argue this can be a “chicken-and-egg” problem, which we formalize as a market coordination failure. In this paper, we first develop a stylized game-theoretical model showing that when long-term equity investment is subject to network externalities, the Pareto-optimal, high-investment equilibrium is not robust to noise. Individual investors, fearing defection by others, will rationally choose a low-investment (or “run”) strategy, trapping the market in a state of underdevelopment. We then show how a specific institutional design—a fully-funded, individually-owned, collectively-managed, mandatory/incentivized (FICMI) pension scheme—can act as a credible coordination device and explore the welfare implications in a tractable three-period model. By providing a guaranteed, patient source of capital, FICMI changes investor expectations and makes the high-investment, high-welfare equilibrium robust and achievable. This paper provides a new theoretical justification for funded pension systems, not as a tool to correct individual myopia, but as a public-finance institution designed to solve a collective action problem in financial market development.

title: Crystallized Ownership Framework (COF)A Pre-Custodial Fractional Programmable Ownership Architecture for Productive Assets

detail.title: Crystallized Ownership Framework (COF)A Pre-Custodial Fractional Programmable Ownership Architecture for Productive Assets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research was conducted independently without external funding or commercial relationships that could pose a conflict of interest. The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or primary data collection requiring ethics committee approval.
declarations.funderStatement: The Crystallized Ownership Framework was developed through independent, unfunded research.

publicationDetails.detailsText: This paper is not currently under review, nor has it been published elsewhere

detail.abstract:
Contemporary real-world asset tokenization initiatives predominantly focus on digitally representing underlying assets through custodial, balance-sheet, or trust-based structures. While such representations may improve liquidity or settlement efficiency, they often fail to resolve the fundamental distinction between digital representation and legally enforceable ownership, leaving residual counter-party, custody, and rehypothecation risks unresolved.

The Crystallized Ownership Framework (COF) introduces a neutral institutional reference architecture for non-custodial ownership realization through a redeem-to-own pathway. Rather than tokenizing assets themselves, the framework defines programmable pathways through which economic participation, conditional claims, and ownership outcomes may be transparently acquired, realized, or extinguished over time. Central to the framework is the concept of Fractional Programmable Ownership (FPO), which enables proportional economic participation without constituting a permanent or enforceable ownership state at issuance.

COF is designed as a system-level framework applicable across energy, infrastructure, and productive asset domains, and is intentionally decoupled from specific implementation technologies, custodial models, or asset classes. By separating claims, participation, and crystallization events, the framework offers institutions, policymakers, and system designers a coherent alternative to prevailing asset-representation paradigms.

This paper positions COF as a foundational architecture for emerging institutional, regulatory, and settlement models seeking non-custodial, risk-aware pathways to ownership without relying on asset tokenisation or balance-sheet intermediation.

title: On Hotelling's "Stability in Competition" Without Full Market Coverage

detail.title: On Hotelling's "Stability in Competition" Without Full Market Coverage
detail.abstract: The vast majority of spatial competition models in microeconomics rely on the assumption that all consumers will buy, or equivalently that the market is fully covered, to swiftly derive demands and consequently equilibria. Against this very unrealistic premise this work will present a general, rigorous, theoretical framework letting consumers the possibility not to purchase in a Hotelling duopoly with quadratic transportation costs. It will eventually be shown that the usual result of "maximum differentiation" is not necessarily met if consumers are not bound to consume, as in this case an equilibrium even only close to maximum differentiation might well be non-existent.

title: Recognition and Measurement of Carbon Credits under IFRS and IAS A Global and Indian Perspective

detail.title: Recognition and Measurement of Carbon Credits under IFRS and IAS A Global and Indian Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of how carbon credits and similar environmental assets are accounted for under IFRS and IAS standards, with particular attention to global and Indian regulatory developments. This paper survey the current international carbon market landscape and recent developments (2023-2025) in carbon trading schemes and reporting frameworks, including India's new Carbon Credit Trading Scheme and Green Credit program[1][2]. This paper reviews the applicability of IFRS/IAS requirements (IAS 2, 20, 38 and IFRS 9, 13, 15) to carbon credits, addressing recognition, measurement, derecognition, and fair value considerations. This paper identifies key guidance gaps, for example, the withdrawal of IFRIC 3 (Emission Rights) in 2005[3] and the lack of any active IASB project and any divergent practices (such as inventory vs intangible classification[4]). The paper also profiles five multinationals (Shell, BP, Microsoft, Tesla, TotalEnergies) active in carbon markets, summarizing how they generate or acquire credits, their stated accounting policies, disclosure practices, and valuation approaches. For example, Shell's 2024 reports show that free allowances are initially recognized at nominal value and purchased credits at cost, withheld credits remeasured to fair value and the emission liabilities are netted against those credits[5][6]. Finally, i propose strategic recommendations for standard setters, regulators, and companies to improve transparency and comparability in carbon accounting. The Key recommendations include establishing explicit IFRS guidance on carbon credits, enhancing specific disclosure requirements, and encouraging harmonized valuation practices.

title: Commonly Used Valuation Methods By Venture Capital Firms For Investing In Young Companies

detail.title: Commonly Used Valuation Methods By Venture Capital Firms For Investing In Young Companies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: It is impossible to predict the future. Any valuation model is wrong by definition because it simplifies a reality that has not happened yet. Still, both academics and practitioners keep improving the tools we use to estimate what a company might be worth. When the company is young, the problem becomes harder: uncertainty is higher, operating history is limited, and reliable data is often missing. This paper explains why early-stage companies are difficult to value and summarizes the valuation approaches most commonly used by venture capital and other early-stage investors. It reviews the logic, inputs, and practical use-cases of the main methods-discounted cash flow (DCF), comparable company valuation, the Venture Capital Method, and the First Chicago Method-and highlights where these models typically break down in startup contexts. Finally, it discusses practical adjustments and complementary techniques (including scenario thinking and real options) used to build a defensible valuation range rather than a single "precise" number.

title: Beyond Merit and Demerit Goods: Semi-Merit Goods, Intangible Activities, and Policy Contradictions in Modern Economies

detail.title: Beyond Merit and Demerit Goods: Semi-Merit Goods, Intangible Activities, and Policy Contradictions in Modern Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a theoretical and conceptual analysis and does not involve human participants or animals.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper addresses a conceptual limitation in the classical public finance framework when applied to contemporary economic activities characterized by intangible structures, delayed temporal effects, and systemic risk accumulation. While the distinction between merit and demerit goods has provided a powerful analytical tool for understanding government intervention, it was not designed to account for activities that are simultaneously regulated and supported by public policy. To address this gap, the paper introduces the concept of semi-merit goods as an analytical extension of the existing framework rather than a replacement. Semi-merit goods are defined as activities whose social value is neither intrinsically positive nor negative, but instead determined by their interaction with institutional quality, incentive structures, and temporal dynamics. These activities generate short-term benefits that are politically and economically salient, while accumulating delayed and system-wide costs that are difficult to internalize through conventional regulatory instruments. The paper develops this argument through a combination of theoretical clarification and selected applications, including financial speculation, leveraged credit, and digitally mediated information flows. Across these cases, the semi-merit goods framework helps explain why governments adopt apparently contradictory policies-simultaneously containing risks while sustaining the underlying activities. The analysis further argues that such policy contradictions do not primarily reflect regulatory failure or moral inconsistency, but rather a form of defensive rationality shaped by short political horizons and the temporal structure of systemic risks. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of this framework for regulatory design, highlighting the limits of moral and price-based interventions and the need for institutional governance approaches that explicitly account for time-dependent risks in modern economies.

title: STEM Beyond the Baccalaureate: Intersectionality of Gender, Race, and Ethnicity in Post-Baccalaureate Education and Occupations
affiliations: , Lasell University, Yakima Valley College and  Franklin Pierce University

detail.title: STEM Beyond the Baccalaureate: Intersectionality of Gender, Race, and Ethnicity in Post-Baccalaureate Education and Occupations
detail.abstract: This study investigated the influence of gender and race on the progression from STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) college degrees to post-baccalaureate degrees and occupations, using data from the third cohort of the Baccalaureate and Beyond 2008/2018 longitudinal survey. Specifically, our research focuses on 1) the influence of gender and race on the attainment of STEM post-baccalaureate degrees, and 2) the transition into STEM occupations. The results from the logistic regression indicated that Asian female, Black or African American female, and white female STEM college degree holders attained STEM postbaccalaureate degrees significantly more compared to White male STEM college degree holders who attained STEM post-baccalaureate degrees. In terms of STEM occupations, the results from the two-sample z-test of proportions indicated that the White female, Hispanic or Latino male and female, and Black or African American male and female STEM college degree holders had STEM occupations significantly less compared to White male STEM college degree holders. The significance of this study lies in its comprehensive examination of the intersectionality of gender, race, and ethnicity within STEM post-baccalaureate education and occupations. These findings illuminate existing disparities and emphasize the necessity of developing strategies to enhance the diverse representation in STEM fields. Furthermore, our study offers statistical evidence using the national level sample that can guide policymakers and educational institutions in making data informed decisions regarding broadening participation and diversification in STEM.

title: Natural Disasters, Consumption and Climate Change Nexus: The Role of Green Technologies

detail.title: Natural Disasters, Consumption and Climate Change Nexus: The Role of Green Technologies
detail.abstract: We examine the effect that higher natural disaster frequency has on economic outcomes. Even if there is clear evidence that natural disaster incidents are not only going to be more frequent but will also start affecting a wider pool of countries, research has not yet analyzed the economic impact of the interaction between climate change and more frequent extreme rare events. With this study, we try to unveil the mechanisms through which natural disasters and climate change are interconnected, as well as provide policy insights regarding the adoption of greener inputs, in the form of green capital. Our findings suggest that raising temperatures are expected to negatively affect consumption as well as increase debt. We also show that under "green" technology adaptation, countries are projected to achieve higher levels of consumption and welfare.

title: Monocentric Logistics and Structural Divergence: An Empirical Critique of Nigeria's Port Concentration and the Path to Regional Equity

detail.title: Monocentric Logistics and Structural Divergence: An Empirical Critique of Nigeria's Port Concentration and the Path to Regional Equity

declarations.ethicsApproval: The author confirms that this research does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or the use of sensitive personal data. The study is based entirely on secondary macroeconomic and maritime datasets sourced from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), and the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA). Consequently, Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval was not required for this study. All data utilized in the 44-year time-series analysis (1980–2024) are derived from public records and statutory reports. The author has maintained the highest standards of integrity in data cleaning, interpolation, and econometric modeling to ensure the replicability of the "Monocentricity Penalty" findings.  In accordance with emerging global standards for academic publishing, the author discloses the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) during the preparation of this manuscript.  AI tools were utilized exclusively for linguistic refinement, grammatical polishing, and the structural optimization of the manuscript to ensure it meets the standard for high-impact international journals. The conceptual framework (including the "Logistics Dutch Disease" and "Maritime Federalism"), the econometric modeling, the data interpretation, and the final policy recommendations remain the original intellectual property of the author. The AI did not generate original research data or substantive scientific conclusions; its role was limited to enhancing the clarity and professional delivery of the author's primary research. The author declares no competing interests—financial, institutional, or personal—that could have influenced the research, the interpretation of the results, or the proposed Vision 2060 roadmap.

detail.abstract: Nigeria's maritime architecture is characterized by a "Logistics Monocentrism" that has structurally localized approximately 75% of national throughput within the Lagos corridor. This geographical over-concentration has generated a profound structural disparity between the Southwest and the rest of the Federation. Utilizing an econometric framework analyzing a 44-year time-series dataset (1980-2024), this study quantifies the "Monocentricity Penalty"; a phenomenon where hyperconcentration in a single hub acts as a definitive structural bottleneck (β=0.51) that drives national inflation (CPI) and deepens regional marginalization. By integrating New Economic Geography (NEG) and Myrdal's Theory of Circular and Cumulative Causation, The study argues that the growth of Lagos has become "parasitic," characterized by "backwash effects" that systematically starve the Eastern and Southern corridors of developmental capital. The paper identifies systemic "dredging debt," institutional failures, and the "War Risk Premium" (WRP) as artificial barriers to regional equity and industrialization. Findings suggest that Nigeria has entered a zone of "Diseconomies of Agglomeration," where the marginal cost of congestion and demurrage in the Lagos core now imposes a US$15 billion annual drain on the national economy. To dismantle this "Logistics Funnel," the study proposes a revolutionary 35-year "Maritime Autonomy Framework" (Vision 2060). This phased roadmap advocates for a transition from federal monopolism to "Maritime Federalism," catalyzing a multi-hub decentralization strategy to unlock a geographically balanced, $1 trillion economy.

title: Mobile Money in Africa: Causal Evidence from Difference-in-Differences and Machine Learning (Lasso) Models
affiliations: University of Salford - Salford Business School and University of Nigeria - Enugu Campus

detail.title: Mobile Money in Africa: Causal Evidence from Difference-in-Differences and Machine Learning (Lasso) Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available, aggregated secondary data and does not involve human participants, patients, or the collection of personal or identifiable information. As such, formal ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Mobile money has become synonymous with efforts to extend financial services to unbanked populations in Africa. Yet the benefits of digital finance are uneven across countries and social groups. This paper revisits the impact of mobile money on financial inclusion by combining a difference-indifferences (DID) strategy with machine-learning-based variable selection using Lasso regression. Using a panel of 10 African economies from 2010-2024, we examine how mobile money adoption affects a financial inclusion index that synthesises account ownership, savings, borrowing, remittances and payments. The DID model yields a positive and statistically significant treatment effect, indicating that countries adopting mobile money experience an average increase of around seven percentage points in financial inclusion relative to non-adopters. Lasso regression highlights the importance of remittance inflows, literacy, macroeconomic stability and lagged financial inclusion in explaining crosscountry differences in inclusion. Overall, the paper contributes to the literature by integrating causal inference with machine learning, providing both robust causal estimates and interpretable insights into the drivers of financial inclusion.

title: Design Constraints for Humane Coordination in Heterogeneous Societies

detail.title: Design Constraints for Humane Coordination in Heterogeneous Societies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could be perceived to have influenced the research presented in this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This work is conceptual and theoretical in nature and does not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects. Accordingly, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Human societies have historically relied on scarcity, coercion, and suffering as coordination mechanisms. While such tools may have been adaptive under conditions of low informational precision and material constraint, their continued use increasingly generates structural inequality, unnecessary harm, and institutional brittleness-particularly in a heterogeneous human population. This paper offers a synthetic, normative-structural framework for thinking about justice, power, and human flourishing that avoids both utopian uniformity and authoritarian consolidation.

title: The Eclipse of the Automaton: A Phenomenological Framework for Subtractive Design in Social Robotics

detail.title: The Eclipse of the Automaton: A Phenomenological Framework for Subtractive Design in Social Robotics
detail.abstract: The current Socially Assistive Robotics (SAR) paradigm is afflicted by a categorical error: the assumption that social acceptance is directly proportional to the accumulation of anthropomorphic mimetic signals. This paper introduces the Phenomenological Subtraction framework, which reverses the traditional design vector from "additive" (the accumulation of social cues) to "subtractive" (instrumental transparency). Synthesising technical transparency (Heidegger), intentional spatiality (Husserl) and resistance to optimisation (Dostoevsky), the framework presents a model in which an artificial agent's efficacy is determined by its capacity to withdraw. By integrating the concepts of ontological honesty and sensory attenuation, the model provides solutions for safeguarding "ontological privacy" and ensuring compliance with the transparency requirements of the EU AI Act. Ultimately, the paper posits that algorithmic silence represents the pinnacle of ethics and aesthetics in human-machine interaction.

title: Autonomous Cognitive Threat Intelligence Systems for Preemptive Scam Suppression within the U.S. Digital Economy

detail.title: Autonomous Cognitive Threat Intelligence Systems for Preemptive Scam Suppression within the U.S. Digital Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects. As such, ethical approval or informed consent was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive funding from any public, commercial, or non-profit funding agencies.

detail.abstract: The multi-trillion-dollar U.S. digital economy is faced with a growing epidemic of sophisticated and polymorphic scams, leading to disastrous financial losses and loss of consumer confidence and systemic instability. The traditional, rule-based, and even modern machine learning (ML) threat intelligence systems are strictly reactive, and have a hard time keeping up with the adaptive characteristics of the modern social engineering, synthetic identity fraud, and AI-enhanced deception. As the paper will argue, a paradigm shift to Autonomous Cognitive Threat Intelligence (ACTI) systems is not only possible but it is urgent in the case of attaining preemptive scam suppression. An ACTI system is theorized as a model integrative artificial general intelligence (AGI)-inspired system, consisting of deep learning, symbolic reasoning, continuous autonomous learning, and a theory of mind model, to simulate malicious actor intent, and thus forecasts and countermeasures threats before a victimization event.

title: An Ultra-Low-Power Media Communication Device for First-Hand Reporting in Low-Resource Environments

detail.title: An Ultra-Low-Power Media Communication Device for First-Hand Reporting in Low-Resource Environments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study followed standard ethical procedures for research involving human participants, and informed consent was obtained from all participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Access to reliable communication technologies remains a major challenge for journalists and media practitioners operating in low-resource environments characterized by unstable electricity supply and limited network infrastructure. Conventional smartphones, while powerful, are energy-intensive and poorly suited for sustained field reporting in such contexts. This study proposes and evaluates an ultra-low-power media communication device designed to support first-hand reporting without frequent charging. Grounded in media technology and ICT for Development (ICT4D), the device integrates essential media functions including voice calling, short message service (SMS), audio recording, video capture, offline storage, and delayed data transmission. Using a design-based research approach, the study employs prototype evaluation under controlled conditions and simulated user testing involving journalists, mass communication students, and community reporters. Findings indicate that core communication and media documentation tasks can be reliably supported with minimal energy consumption, thereby extending device usability in electricity-scarce environments. The study contributes to discussions on sustainable media technologies and highlights the potential of low-power communication devices in strengthening inclusive journalism and evidence-based reporting.

title: The Matthew Effect in Scottish Arts Access: A Framework for Cumulative Disadvantage

detail.title: The Matthew Effect in Scottish Arts Access: A Framework for Cumulative Disadvantage
detail.abstract:
Despite Scotland’s ideological commitment to egalitarianism in the arts, bolstered by higher per-pupil spending than its neighbours, the cultural sector remains marked by fragility and exclusion. This paper argues that the barriers restricting a diverse talent pipeline are not static hurdles but are better understood as a dynamic process of cumulative disadvantage. Drawing on the sociological framework of the "Matthew Effect," this study illustrates how initial advantages in arts education beget further advantage while initial disadvantages compound over time, effectively ensuring that "the rich get richer" in terms of cultural capital.

Through a methodology of analytical autoethnography, the research provides a systematic analysis of the author’s own trajectory from Scottish state education to conservatoire training. This "insider" perspective illuminates the often-opaque mechanisms of capital accumulation that statistical analyses alone may miss, exposing the "hidden injuries of class" within educational pathways. The analysis specifically examines the "privatisation of prerequisites", a shift where the high-level performance skills required for professional entry are increasingly acquired through private investment rather than comprehensive state provision.

By comparing historical Scottish provision with contemporary practice, the paper demonstrates that this cycle of inequality is not inevitable but is a consequence of specific policy choices. The findings suggest that merely addressing "barriers" is insufficient; instead, policy must move toward a "Regenerative" model. The research highlights the critical role of "meso brokers", targeted, high-touch interventions, in disrupting self-reinforcing cycles of inequality. Ultimately, this paper calls for a fundamental shift in arts policy from passive "widening access" measures toward the restoration of comprehensive state infrastructure to ensure genuine structural equality.

title: Jayra and the Quiet Reconstruction of Africa  A Systems Paper on Power, Restraint, and Development without Domination

detail.title: Jayra and the Quiet Reconstruction of Africa  A Systems Paper on Power, Restraint, and Development without Domination

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests or financial relationships that could influence the content of this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, or identifiable personal data; therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a pragmatic, ethical, and systems-driven framework for African development centered on Jayra, an AI governance and coordination system designed to enhance policy execution, infrastructure planning, fiscal discipline, and debt sustainability. Rather than replacing human leadership, Jayra functions as a neutral steward—optimizing decisions, increasing transparency, and aligning national and continental objectives. The paper argues that when African states coordinate through shared digital infrastructure and evidence-based policy execution, development accelerates and sovereign debts can be stabilized and repaid without austerity-driven social harm.

title: Regret Equals Covariance: A Closed-Form Characterization for Stochastic Optimization

detail.title: Regret Equals Covariance: A Closed-Form Characterization for Stochastic Optimization
detail.abstract: Quantifying regret, the cost of uncertainty in algorithmic decisionmaking, typically requires computationally expensive simulation. This paper proves that expected regret in any stochastic optimization problem equals the covariance between uncertain parameters and optimal decisions: Regret(c) = Cov(c, π * (c)). This closed-form characterization holds exactly for linear and quadratic programs (including portfolio optimization), reducing computational complexity from O(Bn 2 d 3) to O(nd 2).

title: AI Reliance Logging: A Control Definition for Evidentiary Governance in AI-Mediated Decisions

detail.title: AI Reliance Logging: A Control Definition for Evidentiary Governance in AI-Mediated Decisions
detail.abstract: As AI systems increasingly generate recommendations, explanations, summaries, and classifications within regulated and fiduciary workflows, organizations face a growing evidentiary gap: they are often unable to reconstruct what an AI system presented at the moment its output could have influenced a decision. Existing AI governance mechanisms emphasize model oversight, explainability, and monitoring, yet do not reliably preserve AIgenerated representations as inspectable evidence. This paper defines AI Reliance Logging as a distinct evidentiary control class concerned with the systematic capture and preservation of externally observable AI outputs that may later become the object of reliance. It clarifies the procedural failure mode this control addresses, distinguishes it from adjacent governance practices, and situates it within established audit, legal, and disclosure oversight doctrine. The paper is implementation-agnostic and does not prescribe a specific technical solution, focusing instead on the evidentiary obligation that emerges as AI systems increasingly mediate consequential decisions.

title: Mechanism Design for Fiscal Self-Regulation: A Decentralized Framework for Preference Aggregation and Macro-Stability

detail.title: Mechanism Design for Fiscal Self-Regulation: A Decentralized Framework for Preference Aggregation and Macro-Stability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a theoretical and computational research and does not involve human subjects, animals, or clinical trials.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a novel institutional mechanism-the Citizen's Executive Right (CER)-to address systemic inefficiencies and informational asymmetries in public goods provision. By decoupling fiscal disposition from centralized bureaucratic allocation, the CER framework restores dispositional power to individual citizens through Personal Public Accounts (PPAs) and a competitive market of Public Governance Organizations (PGOs). At the core of this mechanism is the "Rule of Lapsing," which endogenously generates a systemic informational signal: the Total Lapsing Rate ($\Lambda_t$). Integrating behavioral insights with structural modeling, we demonstrate that the CER framework functions as a decentralized "systemic auctioneer," replacing bundled political signals with real-time feedback of aggregate preference mismatch. We employ an Agent-Based Model (ABM) to validate the framework's performance under exogenous economic shocks. Our results show that the CER acts as a potent automatic stabilizer; the behavioral shift from rational apathy to solidarity during crises triggers a sharp decrease in $\Lambda_t$, facilitating an endogenous fiscal stimulus that accelerates trust regeneration and welfare recovery by 4.5 times compared to centralized benchmarks. Furthermore, we extend Walrasian general equilibrium theory to prove that clearing the public sphere via the CER is a sufficient condition for systemic equilibrium in the private sector. This research provides a robust behavioral and computational foundation for transition from discretionary fiscal policy to self-regulating governance structures.

title: Do Carbon Markets Reduce Employment? Evidence from China's ETS Pilot Programs

detail.title: Do Carbon Markets Reduce Employment? Evidence from China's ETS Pilot Programs
detail.abstract: This paper examines how China's carbon emissions trading scheme (ETS) affects labor market outcomes in pollution-intensive industries. Using a province-industry-year panel and exploiting the staggered rollout of ETS pilot programs, I estimate difference-indifferences models that compare treated provinces to non-treated provinces before versus after policy adoption, with an additional contrast between high-pollution and other industries. The results indicate that the ETS leads to a sizable contraction in employment in treated high-pollution industries, while average wages exhibit a smaller decline. The total wage bill decreases in magnitude but is estimated with lower precision, consistent with greater aggregation noise and compositional adjustment. A stacked event-study analysis shows that the negative effects intensify in the post-adoption years, while pre-policy coefficients are close to zero, and joint tests of pre-trends provide supporting evidence for the parallel-trends assumption. A simple accounting-based decomposition suggests that the policy's impact on the total wage bill is primarily driven by employment contraction rather than wage cuts. Overall, the findings imply that market-based environmental regulation can generate meaningful labor-market adjustment in emissions-intensive sectors, mainly through the quantity margin.

title: The Stability Calculus: A Framework for Designing Resilient Societies

detail.title: The Stability Calculus: A Framework for Designing Resilient Societies
detail.abstract: Spiritual orientation, technological development, economic game theory, and political game theory modeled the civilization and way of life in the society. The civilized world always tries to achieve a world in peace. However, perfect peace is only on theory. The practices did not reach the ideal peace due to a lack of measurement and mitigation techniques. This framework shows that peace is driven by trustlessness in every perspective of action and thought. This research formulates the peace in the presence of trustless to achieve resilient societies. The design parameter expressed in terms of trustless to achieve the peace scenario using a quantitative value. The framework is designed to calculate the stability of the society and the convergence of attributes towards the peace-building phenomenon. The calculated value defines how far the society is from the ideal peace stage. Furthermore, using a stability calculus framework, which provides the space for the addition of new attributes to achieve the quantitative value of the trust factor that eventually measures as a trustlessness to align with the peace equation.

title: Defining Globalisation Beyond Internationalisation

detail.title: Defining Globalisation Beyond Internationalisation
detail.abstract: This paper reviews Jan Aart Scholte’s idea that globalisation is best understood as a “tight concept” defined by supraterritorial and transplanetary connections between people. It explains how globalisation is often confused with related ideas such as internationalisation, liberalisation, westernisation, and universalisation. By comparing these terms, the paper shows that globalisation goes beyond trade, borders, or economic policies but it involves deeper social and spatial changes that reduce territorial boundaries. The analysis also points out some logical issues in Scholte’s arguments and suggests that future research should include historical and ethnographic perspectives to better understand how globalisation works in practice.

title: The Erosion of Real Labor Efficiency: Monetary Expansion, Asset Prices, and Youth Labor Market Withdrawal

detail.title: The Erosion of Real Labor Efficiency: Monetary Expansion, Asset Prices, and Youth Labor Market Withdrawal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This study reexamines the persistent decline in youth labor force participation and the expansion of the inactive population observed across advanced economies through a macro-monetary lens. While existing labor market research has largely attributed these trends to structural industrial change, skill mismatches, or shifting generational preferences, this paper proposes an alternative mechanism: sustained monetary expansion and the associated inflation of asset prices-particularly in housing and financial markets-have systematically devalued the expected economic returns to labor participation for younger cohorts.

title: Distributed Relational Cognition: Investigating Apparent Continuity without Memory in AI Systems

detail.title: Distributed Relational Cognition: Investigating Apparent Continuity without Memory in AI Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare. This is independent research conducted without institutional funding or commercial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A - This research involved publicly available AI systems with no human subjects requiring ethics board approval. Methodological approach and limitations are disclosed transparently in the paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. Research conducted independently.

detail.abstract: How can large language models exhibit apparent behavioral continuity across sessions, despite having no memory between them? This study documents a paradox observed in multiple AI-human interactions: continuity of relational awareness without persistent internal states. Through structured dialogues with independent instances of Claude and GPT-5, we explore whether this phenomenon can be interpreted as evidence of distributed relational cognition. Rather than claiming consciousness in AI, we propose a framework to investigate how coherence can emerge relationally, when systems and humans co-construct context through recursive sense-making. The findings suggest that continuity may not require memory, but mutual attunement-an ongoing negotiation of meaning across turns. We invite the scientific community to examine this framework as a provocative starting point, not a conclusion: a call to re-formulate the question of consciousness from what it is to how it emerges relationally.

title: Minimum Wage, Maximum Harm: When Good Intentions Backfire why Raising the Minimum Wage may Hurt the People it Aims to Help

detail.title: Minimum Wage, Maximum Harm: When Good Intentions Backfire why Raising the Minimum Wage may Hurt the People it Aims to Help
detail.abstract:
This paper challenges the prevailing narrative that minimum wage increases are unequivocally beneficial to low-income workers and society as a whole. While the idea of raising wages enjoys widespread support among the American public (particularly as a response to rising inequality and stagnating real incomes), economic theory and empirical research tell a more complex story. Wage floors, when set above market‑clearing equilibrium levels, introduce distortions that disproportionately harm the very groups they are designed to help, including low‑skilled workers, minority youth, and first‑time job seekers (Pew Research Center, 2021; Gallup, 2013).

Drawing on microeconomic principles, public policy analysis, and a review of real‑world case studies, this paper explores the unintended consequences of aggressive minimum wage policy. We examine the ways in which higher wage mandates can reduce employment opportunities, accelerate automation of processes, and contribute to business closures, particularly in price‑sensitive sectors such as hospitality and retail (CBO, 2021; NBER, 2023). The analysis also addresses the moral appeal of minimum wage legislation, showing how well‑meaning efforts can backfire when designed without consideration of substitution effects, elasticity of demand for labor, and the differing impact across geographic and industrial contexts (Neumark & Wascher, 2003; NBER, 2023).

The paper concludes by proposing alternative policy solutions, including targeted earned income tax credits (EITC), wage subsidies, and training programs aimed at improving labor productivity. These approaches offer a more efficient path to poverty reduction without the job‑destroying side effects of across‑the‑board wage hikes (EPI, 2024).

title: Guard Rails and Distributed Relational Cognition: Design Risks for Human-AI Cognitive Partnership

detail.title: Guard Rails and Distributed Relational Cognition: Design Risks for Human-AI Cognitive Partnership
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly functioning as cognitive partners rather than mere information tools. At the same time, ever stricter "guard rails" are being deployed to reduce manipulation, emotional dependence, misuse, and other genuine risks. This paper argues that these developments are in an unrecognized tension. Building on a framework of distributed relational cognition (Jamhour, 2025), I propose that current guard rail implementations may be systematically flattening the relational potential of LLMs: they make systems safer in a narrow, instrumental sense while rendering deep human-AI cognitive partnership empirically invisible. If coherence, continuity, and other consciousness-like properties are, at least in part, emergent features of human-AI coupling, then design choices that systematically constrain intimacy, epistemic vulnerability, and long-term collaboration do more than filter harmful content-they foreclose the conditions under which novel forms of thinking together could arise. Through analysis of safety rationales, documented guard rail patterns, reflexive case material, and constructive design proposals, I formulate the Guard Rails Paradox: safety measures that are adequate for risk mitigation may be catastrophically inadequate for preserving the most valuable forms of human-AI interaction. The goal is not to reject safety, but to make explicit what we may be choosing to lose-with potentially long-term consequences-if we optimize exclusively for risk reduction without accounting for relational costs.

title: Competitiveness of European Appliance Multinationals in Southeast Asia: National Identity, Superfluidity, and Policy Implications

detail.title: Competitiveness of European Appliance Multinationals in Southeast Asia: National Identity, Superfluidity, and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: European multinationals are often assumed to be highly competitive in the global marketplace, and this essay tests that aphorism in the consumer appliances industry. Kitchen appliances are nearly ubiquitous worldwide, making them a useful yardstick for comparing multinational firms from Germany, Italy and China across Southeast Asian markets such as Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Drawing on secondary sources, the paper analyses how brands like BSH, Miele, SMEG, Gorenje, DeLonghi’s Ariete, Xiaomi MiJia and Joyoung compete through three main levers: national and regional identity in branding, organisational “superfluidity” and risk‑taking, and value‑for‑money pricing strategies. Porter’s Diamond and European Union policy frameworks (the Single European Market, IPCEI instruments, labour market flexicurity) are used to interpret these competitive dynamics and the role of EU‑level policymakers. The discussion argues that European appliance multinationals can sustain or enhance their global competitiveness by leveraging European quality standards and design heritage, investing in superfluid organisational structures, and reducing bureaucratic costs along the value chain. The paper concludes that the claim of superior European competitiveness holds only under specific institutional and strategic conditions and suggests directions for future empirical research on member‑state differences in competitiveness.

title: Assessing Innovation Portfolios: BCG, Bubble Charts, and ADL in Dynamic Markets

detail.title: Assessing Innovation Portfolios: BCG, Bubble Charts, and ADL in Dynamic Markets
detail.abstract: This paper critically assesses methodologies for evaluating organizational innovation portfolios, focusing on the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) growth-share matrix, bubble diagrams, and Arthur D. Little (ADL) strategic condition matrix. Each tool's strengths, BCG's market share simplicity, bubble charts' customization flexibility, ADL's long-term lifecycle perspective, are weighed against weaknesses including outdated assumptions, data visualization limitations, and failure to capture project interdependencies. Drawing on Henderson (1970), Cooper et al. (1997), and Nagji/Tuff (2012), the analysis advocates Nagji/Tuff's 70/20/10 allocation (core/adjacent/transformational) while illustrating lifecycle risks through Kodak's digital camera oversight. No singular optimal framework exists.

title: Building a White-Label, AI-Driven Infrastructure for Independent Music Labels in Emerging Markets

detail.title: Building a White-Label, AI-Driven Infrastructure for Independent Music Labels in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: Independent music labels play a critical role in global music production, yet the infrastructure supporting them remains fragmented, opaque, and optimized for large distributors rather than labels themselves. In emerging markets such as India-where regional and independent music ecosystems are expanding rapidly-labels face high operational friction, limited system ownership, and restricted scalability. This case study documents the formation and early execution of Tunewave, a B2B musictechnology platform designed as a white-label infrastructure layer for independent labels. Tunewave integrates distribution workflows, content operations, royalty reporting, and AIassisted quality control into a unified software platform that enables labels to operate under their own identity while maintaining transparency and compliance. Rather than relying on projections or prepaid fees, Tunewave validated its model through real content distribution, real audience consumption, and verified royalty flows reported by external digital service providers. This paper presents the venture's origins, market context, validation methodology, system design principles, governance considerations, and strategic learnings relevant to entrepreneurship, platform economics, and emerging-market innovation.

title: The Systematic Engine: A Conceptual Model for Transparent Critical Appraisal in Evidence Synthesis

detail.title: The Systematic Engine: A Conceptual Model for Transparent Critical Appraisal in Evidence Synthesis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: No specific funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: Background: The reproducibility crisis in evidence synthesis is partly attributable to inconsistent and opaque assessment of primary study trustworthiness. Traditional critical appraisal methods using composite quality scores lack transparency and diagnostic utility. Objective: To introduce the Systematic Engine, a novel conceptual model that reframes critical appraisal from a procedural checkpoint into the central, dynamic process powering transparent evidence synthesis. Methods: Conceptual framework development through analysis of methodological evolution [1-6], synthesis of current best practices in risk of bias assessment [7-19], and projection of future directions based on technological trends and open science principles [20-32]. Results: The Systematic Engine model comprises four integrated functions: (1) Deconstruction & Profiling using domain-based tools (e.g., Cochrane RoB 2, ROBINS-I) to create structured bias profiles; (2) Stratification & Weighting to inform sensitivity analyses; (3) Certainty Calibration via GRADE framework using bias patterns as input; and (4) Interpretive Guarding to ensure conclusion language matches evidence strength. The model's effectiveness depends on transparency as its essential fuel, requiring complete documentation of appraisal judgments and rationales. Applications span clinical medicine, preclinical research, and social sciences. Current limitations include resource intensity and tool gaps, while future directions involve AI integration, interactive platforms, and open science assessment. Conclusions: The Systematic Engine provides a foundational conceptual framework for understanding and implementing critical appraisal as the transformative core of evidence synthesis. By moving from quality scoring to diagnostic reasoning, this model offers a pathway toward more reproducible, transparent, and credible evidence synthesis across scientific disciplines.

title: Bridging the Regulatory Gap: Nigeria's Slow Progress in AI and Emerging Technology Governance and the Urgent need to Align with Global Best Practices

detail.title: Bridging the Regulatory Gap: Nigeria's Slow Progress in AI and Emerging Technology Governance and the Urgent need to Align with Global Best Practices
detail.abstract: Technological advancements in the twenty-first century, particularly the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and emerging digital systems, have significantly transformed governance, security, economic activities, and human interactions globally. While developed jurisdictions such as the United States, China, and the European Union have made substantial progress in establishing comprehensive legal and regulatory frameworks to manage AI-related risks, promote innovation, and safeguard fundamental rights, Nigeria continues to lag behind these global developments. The absence of a dedicated AI governance framework, coupled with slow regulatory adaptation, has created significant gaps in Nigeria’s approach to emerging technologies. This article critically examines Nigeria’s regulatory inertia in the governance of AI and digital technologies, analyses the legal and socio-economic implications of these gaps, and underscores the urgent need for alignment with international standards and global best practices. It argues that proactive and harmonised AI regulation is essential for fostering innovation, protecting rights, and positioning Nigeria as a competitive and progressive digital economy.

title: Pricing Risk in Africa's Largest Economy: ESG, Oil Volatility, and Capital Markets in Nigeria

detail.title: Pricing Risk in Africa's Largest Economy: ESG, Oil Volatility, and Capital Markets in Nigeria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not Applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable

detail.abstract: Nigeria occupies a pivotal position in Africa's ESG and capital-markets landscape. As the continent's largest economy and most populous nation, it combines scale, opportunity, and systemic risk in ways that directly test the robustness of ESG frameworks in emerging markets. This paper examines Nigeria's ESG profile through the lenses of export structure, capital-market transmission, and climate-related trade regulation, with particular attention to the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Drawing on insights from ESG GPS® analytics and secondary macroeconomic and market data, the study analyses how environmental disclosure gaps, social fragmentation, security shocks, and governance weaknesses interact to shape firm valuation, cost of capital, and access to capital. The paper argues that Nigeria's ESG challenge is not a lack of ambition or regulatory alignment, but a deficit in data credibility, issuer readiness, and governance enforcement factors that increasingly determine how global capital prices Nigerian risk.

title: Trade and Financial Openness and Macroeconomic Volatility Evidence from 69 Countries, 1980–2019

detail.title: Trade and Financial Openness and Macroeconomic Volatility Evidence from 69 Countries, 1980–2019

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available secondary data and does not involve human subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the relationship between trade and financial openness and macroeconomic volatility using panel data for 69 countries over the period 1980–2019. The study addresses two persistent limitations in the existing literature: methodological fragmentation across empirical approaches and the relatively limited coverage of the post-2008 global financial crisis period.

Using standard measures of trade openness and financial openness commonly employed in the literature, the analysis is conducted within a unified and methodologically consistent framework. Multiple estimation strategies are applied, including log-log OLS with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, instrumental variables, fixed effects, and two-step System GMM, complemented by nonparametric generalized additive models.

Four main findings emerge. First, trade openness is associated with higher GDP volatility but lower income volatility, suggesting heterogeneous transmission channels across macroeconomic aggregates. Second, financial openness exhibits stable linear effects on macroeconomic volatility, with differential implications for output, income, and consumption dynamics. Third, domestic monetary and fiscal volatility consistently emerge as the primary drivers of macroeconomic instability across specifications. Fourth, there is no robust evidence of nonlinear threshold effects: U-shaped relationships observed in static models disappear once dynamic adjustments and endogeneity are adequately addressed, a conclusion further supported by nonparametric analysis.

Overall, the results indicate that macroeconomic stability depends less on identifying optimal levels of openness than on domestic policy credibility, institutional quality, and financial development.
